items.name: Robert Walpole
facts: Generally counted as Britain's first Prime Minister, though the title was not official then.
Came to power in 1721 after the South Sea Bubble financial crash of 1720.
Served George I and George II for 21 years, the longest of any Prime Minister.
First PM to live at 10 Downing Street, given to him by George II in 1735.
Kept Britain out of European wars and kept taxes low, following his motto 'let sleeping dogs lie'.
Was pushed into the War of Jenkins' Ear with Spain in 1739 against his wishes.
Resigned in 1742 after losing a Commons vote and became Earl of Orford.

items.name: Earl of Wilmington
facts: Born Spencer Compton; he was a former Speaker of the House of Commons.
Succeeded Walpole in 1742 as a figurehead while Lord Carteret held the real power.
Britain was fighting in the War of the Austrian Succession during his term.
Died in office in July 1743 and was succeeded by Henry Pelham.

items.name: Henry Pelham
facts: Younger brother of the Duke of Newcastle, who served in his government.
His government survived the Jacobite rising of 1745 led by Bonnie Prince Charlie.
Ended Britain's part in the War of the Austrian Succession at Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748.
Britain switched to the Gregorian calendar in 1752, skipping eleven days in September.
Cut the national debt and the interest paid on it during years of peace.
Died in office in 1754; George II said 'Now I shall have no more peace'.

items.name: Duke of Newcastle
facts: Thomas Pelham-Holles succeeded his brother Henry Pelham in 1754.
A master of patronage who had already been Secretary of State for thirty years.
Resigned in 1756 after the loss of Minorca at the start of the Seven Years' War.
Returned in 1757 in a famous partnership with Pitt the Elder, who ran the war.
Served two terms and resigned in 1762 after falling out with the new king, George III.

items.name: Duke of Devonshire
facts: William Cavendish, 4th Duke of Devonshire, took office in November 1756.
His government was really led by Pitt the Elder as Secretary of State.
Lasted only about seven months, in the early years of the Seven Years' War.
Admiral Byng was shot in 1757 for failing to save Minorca, during his term.

items.name: Earl of Bute
facts: John Stuart, a Scottish peer who had been tutor and favourite of the young George III.
The first Scottish Prime Minister; widely disliked and mocked in England.
Negotiated the Treaty of Paris in 1763, which ended the Seven Years' War.
Resigned in 1763 after his unpopular cider tax caused protests and riots.

items.name: George Grenville
facts: Brother-in-law of Pitt the Elder and father of a later PM, Lord Grenville.
Introduced the Stamp Act of 1765 to tax the American colonies, sparking colonial anger.
Prosecuted the radical John Wilkes in 1763 for criticising the king's speech.
George III found him dull and lecturing, and dismissed him in 1765.

items.name: Marquess of Rockingham
facts: Charles Watson-Wentworth, a wealthy Yorkshire landowner who loved horse racing.
Repealed the hated Stamp Act in 1766 to calm the American colonies.
Edmund Burke was his private secretary and closest political ally.
Returned in 1782 to open peace talks with the Americans after the defeat at Yorktown.
Served twice; died of influenza only fourteen weeks into his second term in 1782.

items.name: William Pitt the Elder
facts: Known as 'the Great Commoner' until he became Earl of Chatham in 1766.
As Secretary of State from 1757 he led Britain to victory in the Seven Years' War.
Famous for 1759, the 'year of victories', when Britain took Quebec from France.
Became Prime Minister in 1766, but gout and ill health left him unable to govern.
Opposed harsh treatment of the American colonies and called for peace with them.
Collapsed in the House of Lords during a speech in 1778 and died weeks later.
Father of William Pitt the Younger, who became PM in 1783.

items.name: Duke of Grafton
facts: Augustus FitzRoy, a descendant of Charles II, took over when Chatham fell ill.
Attacked in the anonymous 'Letters of Junius' over his politics and private life.
His government kept the tea duty in America, which made colonial unrest worse.
Resigned in January 1770 and was succeeded by Lord North.

items.name: Lord North
facts: Frederick North served George III for twelve years and was a loyal servant of the king.
Kept the tea duty, which led to the Boston Tea Party in 1773.
Passed the 'Intolerable Acts' in 1774 to punish Massachusetts.
Prime Minister throughout the American War of Independence, which began in 1775.
When news of the defeat at Yorktown came in 1781 he said 'Oh God, it is all over'.
Forced out by Parliament in 1782, the first PM to fall to a no-confidence vote.
Later formed a notorious coalition with his old enemy Charles James Fox in 1783.

items.name: Earl of Shelburne
facts: William Petty took over when Rockingham died in July 1782.
Negotiated the Treaty of Paris of 1783, which recognised American independence.
Nicknamed 'the Jesuit of Berkeley Square' for his reputation for cunning.
Lost office in 1783 when Fox and North joined forces against him.

items.name: Duke of Portland
facts: William Cavendish-Bentinck served two terms, 24 years apart.
In 1783 he was the figurehead of the Fox-North coalition, which George III hated.
George III dismissed the coalition in December 1783 over Fox's India Bill.
Returned in 1807 as a Tory, aged 69 and in poor health.
His second government began the Peninsular War against Napoleon in Spain and Portugal.
Resigned in 1809 after his ministers Canning and Castlereagh fought a duel.

items.name: William Pitt the Younger
facts: Became Prime Minister in December 1783 aged just 24, the youngest ever.
Son of Pitt the Elder; served George III through the king's bouts of madness.
Led Britain in war against revolutionary France from 1793.
Introduced income tax in 1799 to pay for the war.
His Act of Union with Ireland created the United Kingdom in 1801.
Resigned in 1801 when George III refused to allow Catholic emancipation.
Returned in 1804 and died in office in 1806, soon after Napoleon's victory at Austerlitz.

items.name: Henry Addington
facts: A former Speaker of the Commons and the son of Pitt the Younger's doctor.
Made the Peace of Amiens with France in 1802, which lasted barely a year.
Mocked in the rhyme 'Pitt is to Addington as London is to Paddington'.
Resigned in 1804 as war with Napoleon resumed, and Pitt returned.
Later, as Lord Sidmouth, he was Home Secretary at the time of Peterloo in 1819.

items.name: Lord Grenville
facts: William Grenville, son of George Grenville and cousin of Pitt the Younger.
Led the 'Ministry of All the Talents' after Pitt's death in 1806.
His government abolished the slave trade across the British Empire in 1807.
Dismissed by George III in 1807 after proposing to let Catholics hold army commissions.

items.name: Spencer Perceval
facts: A devout evangelical lawyer with twelve children.
Served during the final madness of George III; the Regency began in 1811.
Kept up the Peninsular War under Wellington against Napoleon's armies.
The only British Prime Minister to be assassinated.
Shot dead in the lobby of the Commons by John Bellingham on 11 May 1812.

items.name: Lord Liverpool
facts: Robert Jenkinson served fifteen years, longer than any PM since Pitt the Younger.
Took office in 1812 after Perceval's assassination.
Fought the War of 1812 against the United States.
Led Britain to final victory over Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815.
Introduced the Corn Laws in 1815 to keep grain prices high for farmers.
The Peterloo Massacre of 1819 and the harsh 'Six Acts' happened under him.
Suffered a stroke in 1827 and resigned; succeeded by George Canning.

items.name: George Canning
facts: Prime Minister for only 119 days in 1827, the shortest term until Liz Truss in 2022.
Had fought a duel with Castlereagh in 1809 and was wounded in the thigh.
As Foreign Secretary he backed independence for Spain's colonies in South America.
Many Tories, including Wellington and Peel, refused to serve under him.
Died in office in August 1827 and was succeeded by Goderich.

items.name: Viscount Goderich
facts: Frederick Robinson, nicknamed 'Prosperity Robinson' when he was Chancellor.
Took over after Canning's death but could not hold his cabinet together.
Resigned after about 130 days in January 1828, reportedly in tears before George IV.
Never faced Parliament as Prime Minister; later became Earl of Ripon.

items.name: Duke of Wellington
facts: Arthur Wellesley, the general who defeated Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815.
Nicknamed 'the Iron Duke'; served George IV and William IV.
Passed Catholic Emancipation in 1829, letting Catholics sit in Parliament.
Fought a duel with the Earl of Winchilsea in 1829 over Catholic Emancipation.
Opposed parliamentary reform, and his government fell in 1830.
Served briefly again as caretaker in late 1834 until Peel could take over.

items.name: Earl Grey
facts: Charles Grey led the Whigs back to power after decades of Tory rule.
Passed the Great Reform Act of 1832, which widened the vote and abolished rotten boroughs.
His government abolished slavery across most of the British Empire in 1833.
The Factory Act of 1833 limited child labour in textile mills.
Earl Grey tea is said to be named after him.
Resigned in 1834 over Irish policy and was succeeded by Melbourne.

items.name: Lord Melbourne
facts: William Lamb, husband of Lady Caroline Lamb, who had a famous affair with Byron.
As Home Secretary in 1834 he let the Tolpuddle Martyrs be transported to Australia.
Dismissed by William IV in 1834, the last time a monarch sacked a Prime Minister.
Returned in 1835 and became a mentor and father figure to the young Queen Victoria from 1837.
The 'Bedchamber Crisis' of 1839 kept him in office when Peel refused to form a government.
Resigned in 1841 after losing the general election to Peel.
The city of Melbourne in Australia is named after him.

items.name: Robert Peel
facts: As Home Secretary he founded the Metropolitan Police in 1829; officers were called 'bobbies' or 'peelers'.
His Tamworth Manifesto of 1834 is seen as the founding of the Conservative Party.
Served two terms, under William IV and then Queen Victoria.
Brought back income tax in 1842, in peacetime.
Repealed the Corn Laws in 1846 during the Irish Famine, splitting his party.
His followers, the Peelites, included the young William Gladstone.
Died in 1850 after falling from his horse on Constitution Hill in London.

items.name: Lord John Russell
facts: Son of the Duke of Bedford; he helped to draft the Great Reform Act of 1832.
Became PM in 1846 after Peel fell over the Corn Laws.
His government's response to the Irish Famine is widely seen as inadequate.
The Great Exhibition was held in London in 1851 during his first term.
Served twice; his short second term as Earl Russell fell over a reform bill in 1866.
Grandfather of the philosopher Bertrand Russell.

items.name: Earl of Derby
facts: Edward Stanley led the Conservative Party for 22 years, longer than anyone else.
Served three times, each time heading a minority government.
His 1852 cabinet was nicknamed the 'Who? Who?' ministry after the deaf Wellington's comments.
Disraeli was his Chancellor in all three governments.
His third government passed the Second Reform Act of 1867, giving many working men the vote.
Resigned through ill health in 1868 and Disraeli succeeded him.
The Derby horse race is named after his ancestor, the 12th Earl.

items.name: Earl of Aberdeen
facts: George Hamilton-Gordon led a coalition of Peelites, Whigs and Radicals from 1852.
Gladstone was his Chancellor and produced a famous free-trade budget in 1853.
Led Britain into the Crimean War against Russia in 1854.
Blamed for the poor management of the war and the suffering of the troops.
Resigned in 1855 after losing a Commons vote calling for an inquiry into the war.

items.name: Lord Palmerston
facts: Henry John Temple, nicknamed 'Pam' and 'Lord Cupid' because of his love affairs.
Became PM in 1855 aged 70 to win the Crimean War, ended by the Treaty of Paris in 1856.
Famous for 'gunboat diplomacy'; said Britain had no permanent allies, only permanent interests.
His first government dealt with the Indian Mutiny of 1857.
His second government, from 1859, is seen as the first Liberal government.
Kept Britain neutral during the American Civil War.
Died in office in October 1865 aged 80, the last PM to die in office.

items.name: Benjamin Disraeli
facts: A novelist of Jewish birth, baptised a Christian as a boy; nicknamed 'Dizzy'.
Great rival of Gladstone; Queen Victoria much preferred Disraeli.
On becoming PM in 1868 he said 'I have climbed to the top of the greasy pole'.
Bought Britain a large share in the Suez Canal in 1875.
Made Victoria Empress of India in 1876 and became Earl of Beaconsfield the same year.
His second government passed reforms on public health, housing and trade unions in 1875.
Returned from the Congress of Berlin in 1878 claiming 'peace with honour'; lost the 1880 election.

items.name: William Gladstone
facts: Served four terms, more than any other PM, and was 84 when he retired in 1894.
Nicknamed 'the Grand Old Man' or 'GOM'; Disraeli said it stood for 'God's Only Mistake'.
His first government passed the Education Act of 1870 and the Secret Ballot Act of 1872.
The Third Reform Act of 1884 gave the vote to rural working men.
Blamed for the death of General Gordon at Khartoum in 1885.
Twice failed to pass Home Rule for Ireland, in 1886 and 1893, splitting the Liberals.
Queen Victoria complained that he spoke to her 'as if I were a public meeting'.

items.name: Lord Salisbury
facts: Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, the last PM to govern from the House of Lords.
Served three terms, over thirteen years in all, often acting as his own Foreign Secretary.
His time saw the 'Scramble for Africa' and the policy known as 'splendid isolation'.
Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee of 1897 took place during his third term.
Led Britain into the Boer War in South Africa, which ran from 1899 to 1902.
Victoria died in 1901 and he served Edward VII until retiring in 1902.
Was succeeded by his nephew Arthur Balfour, which some say gave us the phrase 'Bob's your uncle'.

items.name: Earl of Rosebery
facts: Archibald Primrose was chosen by Queen Victoria to replace Gladstone in 1894.
Married a Rothschild heiress and owned racehorses; his horses won the Derby in 1894 and 1895.
Led a divided Liberal government from the Lords for only about fifteen months.
Resigned in 1895 after a Commons defeat over army supplies of cordite.

groups.name: Edwardian era and the World Wars

items.name: Arthur Balfour
facts: Nephew of Lord Salisbury, whom he succeeded in 1902 under Edward VII.
His Education Act of 1902 put state schools under local councils.
The Entente Cordiale with France was signed in 1904 during his term.
His party split over Joseph Chamberlain's campaign for tariff reform.
Resigned in December 1905 and lost the 1906 election in a Liberal landslide.
As Foreign Secretary he issued the Balfour Declaration of 1917 supporting a Jewish homeland in Palestine.

items.name: Henry Campbell-Bannerman
facts: The first man to be officially called 'Prime Minister', from 1905.
Won the 1906 general election in a landslide for the Liberals.
Gave self-government to the defeated Boer republics in 1906 and 1907.
The Trade Disputes Act of 1906 protected unions from being sued over strikes.
Resigned through ill health in April 1908 and died at 10 Downing Street days later.

items.name: H. H. Asquith
facts: Herbert Henry Asquith took over from Campbell-Bannerman in 1908.
His government introduced old age pensions in 1908 and National Insurance in 1911.
Lloyd George's 'People's Budget' of 1909 was thrown out by the House of Lords.
The Parliament Act of 1911 ended the Lords' power to veto money bills.
Faced suffragette protests, big strikes and the crisis over Irish Home Rule.
Took Britain into the First World War in August 1914.
Pushed out by Lloyd George in December 1916 amid criticism of the war effort.

items.name: David Lloyd George
facts: The only Welsh-speaking Prime Minister; nicknamed 'the Welsh Wizard'.
Led a coalition with the Conservatives to victory in the First World War in 1918.
Won the 1918 'coupon election' promising 'a land fit for heroes'.
Negotiated the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 with Wilson and Clemenceau.
Signed the Anglo-Irish Treaty in 1921, which created the Irish Free State.
Scandal over selling honours for cash damaged his reputation.
Fell in 1922 when Conservative MPs voted at the Carlton Club to end the coalition; the last Liberal PM.

items.name: Bonar Law
facts: Andrew Bonar Law was born in New Brunswick, Canada, the only PM born outside the British Isles.
Grew up in Glasgow and made his fortune in the iron trade.
Became PM in October 1922 after the Conservatives left Lloyd George's coalition.
Asquith called him 'the Unknown Prime Minister'.
Resigned after only 209 days in May 1923 because of throat cancer, and died that October.

items.name: Stanley Baldwin
facts: A Worcestershire ironmaster and a cousin of Rudyard Kipling.
Served three terms under George V, Edward VIII and George VI.
Faced the General Strike of 1926, which collapsed after nine days.
Gave the vote to all women over 21 in 1928, the so-called 'flapper vote'.
Attacked the press barons in 1931 for wanting 'power without responsibility'.
Handled the abdication crisis of 1936 when Edward VIII gave up the throne for Wallis Simpson.
Retired in 1937; later blamed for slow rearmament against Hitler.

items.name: Ramsay MacDonald
facts: Illegitimate son of a Scottish farm worker; the first Labour Prime Minister in 1924.
His first minority government lasted nine months and fell amid the 'Zinoviev letter' affair.
Returned in 1929, just before the Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression.
Split Labour in 1931 by forming a National Government with the Conservatives to cut spending.
Expelled from the Labour Party, which branded him a traitor.
Britain left the gold standard in 1931 under his National Government.
Handed over to Baldwin in 1935 as his health failed.

items.name: Neville Chamberlain
facts: Son of Joseph Chamberlain and half-brother of Austen; a Birmingham businessman and former Chancellor.
Succeeded Baldwin in 1937 under George VI.
Followed a policy of appeasement towards Hitler.
Signed the Munich Agreement in 1938, giving Hitler the Sudetenland, and promised 'peace for our time'.
Declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939 after the invasion of Poland.
Resigned in May 1940 after the Norway debate, where Leo Amery told him 'In the name of God, go'.
Died of cancer in November 1940, six months after leaving office.

items.name: Winston Churchill
facts: Became PM on 10 May 1940, the day Germany invaded France and the Low Countries.
Led the wartime coalition; famous for 'blood, toil, tears and sweat' and 'we shall fight on the beaches'.
Worked with Roosevelt and Stalin to win the Second World War in 1945.
Lost the 1945 election to Attlee despite victory in Europe.
Coined the phrase 'Iron Curtain' in a speech at Fulton, Missouri, in 1946.
Returned in 1951 aged 76; won the Nobel Prize for Literature and a knighthood in 1953.
Resigned in 1955 in favour of Eden; given a state funeral in 1965.

items.name: Clement Attlee
facts: Won Labour's first majority in a landslide in July 1945, defeating Churchill.
Created the National Health Service in 1948, with Aneurin Bevan as Health Minister.
Built the welfare state along the lines of the Beveridge Report.
Nationalised coal, railways, steel and the Bank of England.
Granted independence to India and Pakistan in 1947.
Britain joined NATO in 1949 and built its own atomic bomb.
Narrowly lost the 1951 election to Churchill.

items.name: Anthony Eden
facts: Churchill's long-serving Foreign Secretary, who waited years for the top job.
Married Churchill's niece Clarissa in 1952.
Won the 1955 general election soon after taking office.
Ordered the invasion of Suez in 1956 after Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal.
Forced into a humiliating withdrawal by American pressure and a run on the pound.
Resigned in January 1957 citing ill health; succeeded by Macmillan.

items.name: Harold Macmillan
facts: Nicknamed 'Supermac' by the cartoonist Vicky.
Told voters in 1957 that 'most of our people have never had it so good'.
Won the 1959 election with a bigger majority.
His 'wind of change' speech in Cape Town in 1960 signalled the end of empire in Africa.
Sacked a third of his cabinet in the 'Night of the Long Knives' in July 1962.
De Gaulle vetoed Britain's first bid to join the Common Market in 1963.
Resigned in October 1963 after the Profumo affair and a prostate operation.

items.name: Alec Douglas-Home
facts: The 14th Earl of Home gave up his peerage to become PM in October 1963.
Chosen by a secretive 'magic circle' of senior Tories rather than by a vote.
Harold Wilson mocked him as the '14th Earl'; he replied that Wilson was 'the 14th Mr Wilson'.
The only PM to have played first-class cricket.
Lost the October 1964 election narrowly to Labour after a year in office.
Later served as Heath's Foreign Secretary from 1970 to 1974.

items.name: Harold Wilson
facts: A grammar school boy from Huddersfield, famous for his pipe and Gannex raincoat.
Won four general elections: 1964, 1966 and both of 1974.
Promised to forge a new Britain in the 'white heat' of technology.
Devalued the pound in 1967, saying it would not hit 'the pound in your pocket'.
His first government saw the end of the death penalty and the legalising of abortion and homosexuality.
Refused to send British troops to Vietnam, and won the 1975 referendum to stay in the Common Market.
Resigned unexpectedly in March 1976, aged 60, and was succeeded by Callaghan.

items.name: Edward Heath
facts: A grammar school boy from Kent; a keen yachtsman and musician who never married.
Won the 1970 election unexpectedly against Wilson.
Took Britain into the European Economic Community on 1 January 1973.
Imposed direct rule on Northern Ireland in 1972 after Bloody Sunday.
Miners' strikes and the oil crisis led to the three-day week in early 1974.
Called an election in February 1974 asking 'Who governs Britain?' and lost.
Ousted as party leader by Margaret Thatcher in 1975, then sulked for decades.

items.name: James Callaghan
facts: The only person to hold all four great offices: Chancellor, Home Secretary, Foreign Secretary and PM.
Nicknamed 'Sunny Jim'; he had served in the navy in the Second World War.
Took over from Wilson in 1976; the IMF loan crisis followed later that year.
The Lib-Lab pact of 1977 kept his minority government in power.
The 'Winter of Discontent' of 1978 to 1979 brought strikes and uncollected rubbish.
The Sun headline 'Crisis? What crisis?' was pinned on him, though he never said it.
Lost a confidence vote by a single vote in March 1979, then lost the election to Thatcher.

items.name: Margaret Thatcher
facts: The first woman Prime Minister; a grocer's daughter from Grantham.
Nicknamed 'the Iron Lady' by a Soviet newspaper; told her party 'the lady's not for turning' in 1980.
Won the Falklands War against Argentina in 1982.
Survived the IRA bomb at the Grand Hotel in Brighton in 1984.
Defeated the miners' strike of 1984 to 1985, led by Arthur Scargill.
Privatised state industries such as British Telecom and British Gas, and sold council houses.
Resigned in November 1990 after the poll tax and a leadership challenge by Michael Heseltine.

items.name: John Major
facts: Left school at 16 and worked in banking; son of a music hall performer.
Won the 1992 election with more votes than any party had ever received.
On 'Black Wednesday' in September 1992 the pound crashed out of the ERM.
Negotiated opt-outs from the Maastricht Treaty, but Eurosceptic rebels tore his party apart.
Began the Northern Ireland peace process with the Downing Street Declaration in 1993.
His 'Back to Basics' campaign was undermined by a string of sleaze scandals.
Lost the 1997 election to Tony Blair in a landslide.

items.name: Tony Blair
facts: His 1997 landslide ended 18 years of Conservative rule; he won again in 2001 and 2005.
Rebranded the party as 'New Labour' and dropped Clause IV on nationalisation.
Called Diana 'the People's Princess' after her death in 1997.
Signed the Good Friday Agreement in 1998, bringing peace to Northern Ireland.
Created the Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly in 1999, and introduced the minimum wage.
Took Britain into the Iraq War in 2003, his most controversial decision.
Stepped down in June 2007 and handed over to Gordon Brown.

items.name: Gordon Brown
facts: Chancellor for ten years under Blair before succeeding him in June 2007.
Son of a Church of Scotland minister; lost the sight of one eye playing rugby.
Decided against an early election in autumn 2007, which damaged his standing.
Led the response to the 2008 financial crisis, bailing out banks such as RBS.
Hosted the G20 summit in London in 2009.
Was caught on a microphone calling a voter a 'bigoted woman' during the 2010 campaign.
Lost the 2010 election, which produced a hung parliament and the Cameron-Clegg coalition.

items.name: David Cameron
facts: Became PM in 2010 aged 43, leading the first coalition since 1945 with Nick Clegg's Liberal Democrats.
Brought in austerity with Chancellor George Osborne to cut the deficit.
Legalised same-sex marriage in England and Wales in 2013.
Won the 2014 Scottish independence referendum for the Union.
After winning a majority in 2015, he called the EU referendum of June 2016.
Campaigned to Remain and lost by 52 to 48; announced his resignation the next morning.
Succeeded by Theresa May in July 2016; later returned as Foreign Secretary under Sunak in 2023.

items.name: Theresa May
facts: The second woman PM; a vicar's daughter who had been Home Secretary for six years.
Took office in July 2016 after the Brexit vote, saying 'Brexit means Brexit'.
Called a snap election in 2017 and lost her majority, relying on the DUP.
Faced the Grenfell Tower fire in 2017 and the Salisbury poisonings in 2018.
MPs rejected her Brexit withdrawal agreement three times in 2019.
Remembered for the slogan 'strong and stable' and for dancing on stage at conference in 2018.
Announced her resignation in tears in May 2019 and was succeeded by Boris Johnson in July.

items.name: Boris Johnson
facts: Mayor of London from 2008 to 2016 and a leader of the Vote Leave campaign.
Won the December 2019 election with an 80-seat majority on the slogan 'Get Brexit Done'.
Britain left the European Union on 31 January 2020.
Led the country through the Covid-19 pandemic and was himself in intensive care in April 2020.
The 'Partygate' scandal over lockdown gatherings in Downing Street brought him a police fine in 2022.
A strong supporter of Ukraine after Russia's invasion in February 2022.
Resigned in July 2022 after dozens of ministers quit over the Chris Pincher affair.

items.name: Liz Truss
facts: The shortest-serving PM, with just 49 days in office.
The last PM appointed by Elizabeth II, two days before the Queen died in September 2022.
Her 'mini-budget' of unfunded tax cuts with Chancellor Kwasi Kwarteng sent the pound and pension funds into crisis.
Sacked Kwarteng and reversed most of the tax cuts within weeks.
Famously outlasted by a lettuce in a Daily Star stunt.
Resigned in October 2022 and was succeeded by Rishi Sunak.

items.name: Rishi Sunak
facts: The first British Asian and first Hindu PM, and the first appointed by Charles III.
Took office aged 42, the youngest PM for over 200 years.
As Chancellor during Covid he created the furlough scheme in 2020.
Became leader unopposed in October 2022 after Truss resigned.
Agreed the Windsor Framework with the EU on Northern Ireland trade in 2023.
His Rwanda asylum plan was ruled unlawful by the Supreme Court in 2023.
Called a surprise election in the rain in May 2024 and lost in a Labour landslide.

items.name: Keir Starmer
facts: Named after Keir Hardie, Labour's first leader.
A former Director of Public Prosecutions, knighted in 2014; first became an MP in 2015 aged 52.
Won the July 2024 election in a landslide, with over 400 seats, ending 14 years of Conservative rule.
The first Labour PM since Gordon Brown left office in 2010.
Faced riots in summer 2024 after the Southport stabbings.
Cut winter fuel payments for most pensioners in 2024, then partly reversed the cut in 2025.
